newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal unflinching on EMU entry goal - Guterres.
newsitem.headline: Portugal unflinching on EMU entry goal - Guterres.

text.p: Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said on Tuesday that Portugal remained "unflinching" in its determination to join the European Union's single currency at its launch in 1999.

In a statement issued after Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm reportedly cast doubts on Lisbon's ability to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) from the start, Guterres said that the presence of the escudo would not weaken the euro, the future single currency.
"A strong euro is perfectly compatible with the presence of the escudo (in monetary union)," Guterres said.

"The escudo is one of the most stable currencies in the European Monetary System (EMS), reflecting an economy that is amongst those that have moved towards EMU convergence criteria in the most consistent, sustained and sustainable fashion," he said.

Portuguese financial daily Diario Economico had earlier reported Zalm, who will preside at meetings of EU finance ministers for the next six months, had expressed serious doubts about whether Portugal would qualify for EMU from the beginning.
It said that Zalm, who gave a briefing to Brussels-based journalists in The Hague on Monday, had excluded Portugal from a "hard core" of EU countries to take part in the launch.
"The Portuguese government remains unflinching in its decision (to seek to join EMU) and (financial) markets will be confident (that it can)," Guterres said.
Guterres said that if a country met entry targets for EMU, as laid down in the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, then it would have to be admitted.

"The Maastricht Treaty lays down objective criteria for entry to the single currency. These criteria have nothing to do with geographic location but with the solidity and sustainability of a country's economic indicators," he said.
Portugal's parliament recently approved the Socialist government's 1997 budget plan calling for a deficit of 2.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), inside the three percent EMU ceiling.
